prompt: What is the key difference between a container and a virtual machine?
explanation: A container is an isolated process that shares the host kernel, so it is lightweight. A VM runs a full guest OS on a hypervisor, which is heavier.

options.text: A container includes its own full operating system, a VM does not
A container shares the host's kernel and is an isolated process; a VM runs its own guest OS on a hypervisor
There is no difference; the words are interchangeable
A VM is always smaller and faster than a container

prompt: Which statement correctly describes images and containers?
explanation: An image is a read-only template. A container is a running instance created from an image, with a thin writable layer added on top. One image can produce many containers.

options.text: An image is a running process; a container is a template
An image is a read-only template; a container is a running instance of that image
Each image can produce exactly one container
Containers are stored in registries; images are not

prompt: Which of the following are parts of the Docker architecture? Select all that apply.
explanation: The client talks to the daemon, which runs containers and pulls or pushes images to a registry. Docker runs locally; no remote cloud account is required.

options.text: The docker command-line client
The dockerd daemon
A registry such as Docker Hub
A required cloud account that runs your containers remotely

prompt: Because Docker builds images that follow the ______ standard, they also run on other compliant tools. (three-letter acronym)
explanation: The Open Container Initiative (OCI) standardizes the image and runtime formats, which is what makes images portable across compliant tools.

prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
explanation: The image is the template, a container is a running instance, a registry stores images, and dockerd is the engine doing the work.

pairs.right: A read-only template used to create containers
A running, isolated instance of an image
A service that stores and distributes images
The daemon that builds images and runs containers

prompt: You run `docker run nginx` and the image is not on your machine yet. Order what happens.
explanation: The client hands the command to the daemon, which pulls the missing image, creates a container from it, and starts the process.

items.text: The docker client sends the command to the daemon
The daemon pulls the nginx image from the registry
The daemon creates a container from the image

prompt: On macOS and Windows, how does Docker Desktop run Linux containers?
explanation: macOS and Windows have no Linux kernel, so Docker Desktop runs Docker Engine inside a lightweight managed Linux VM. Linux containers run in that VM.

options.text: It rewrites the containers to run natively on macOS or Windows
It runs Docker Engine inside a small managed Linux virtual machine
It requires you to install a separate Linux computer
It cannot run Linux containers at all

prompt: Why does `docker run hello-world` exit almost immediately?
explanation: A container lives only as long as its main process. hello-world prints a message and its process finishes, so the container exits right away — that is expected.

options.text: Because the image failed to download
Because a container runs only as long as its main process, and hello-world's process just prints and ends
Because hello-world is broken
Because you forgot the -d flag

prompt: You ran a container and it is not shown by `docker ps`. How do you see it?
explanation: docker ps shows only running containers. docker ps -a shows all of them, including stopped (exited) ones.

options.text: docker ps -a, which lists all containers including exited ones
docker images, which lists containers
It is gone forever and cannot be seen
docker version

prompt: To run a container in the background instead of the foreground, add the ______ flag to docker run. (include the dash)
explanation: -d (or --detach) runs the container detached, in the background, so it does not tie up your terminal.

prompt: Which statements about the container lifecycle are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: An exited container persists (with its writable layer) until docker rm removes it, and docker start can restart it. The writable layer is not deleted on exit — only on removal.

options.text: A stopped (exited) container still exists until you remove it
docker start can run a stopped container again
docker rm deletes a container
Once a container exits, its writable layer is instantly deleted

prompt: Order these commands to run nginx in the background and then clean it up.
explanation: Start it detached, confirm it is running, stop the process, then remove the container.

prompt: How should you read the flag `-p 8080:80`?
explanation: The format is host:container. -p 8080:80 forwards traffic from port 8080 on your machine to port 80 inside the container.

options.text: container port 8080 maps to host port 80
host port 8080 maps to container port 80
both ports must always be identical
it blocks port 8080 on the host

prompt: Which command opens an interactive shell inside a running container named web?
explanation: docker exec runs a new command inside a running container; -it makes it interactive with a terminal. docker run would create a new container instead.

options.text: docker run -it web sh
docker exec -it web sh
docker logs -it web sh
docker shell web

prompt: Why is docker exec usually preferred over docker attach for debugging?
explanation: exec launches a new process (like a shell); exiting it leaves the container running. attach connects to the main process, so Ctrl+C can terminate the whole container.

options.text: attach is faster but insecure
exec starts a separate process, so leaving it does not stop the container, while attach connects to the main process where Ctrl+C can stop it
attach cannot open a shell at all
there is no difference

prompt: To stream a container's output live, run docker ______ -f <container>. (one word)
explanation: docker logs -f follows the container's output, streaming new lines until you stop it with Ctrl+C.

prompt: Which statements about stopping and removing containers are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: stop is graceful, rm removes a stopped container, and rm -f forces removal of a running one. --rm does the opposite of (d): it auto-removes the container on exit.

options.text: docker stop asks the process to shut down gracefully before forcing it
docker rm removes a stopped container
docker rm -f can remove a running container
--rm keeps the container forever after it exits

prompt: Order these commands to run, inspect, and clean up a web server.
explanation: Start the container, read its logs, step inside to look around, then force-remove it when you are done.

prompt: What is the difference between ARG and ENV?
explanation: ARG exists only during the build and is not present in the running container. ENV is baked into the image and available to the process at run time.

options.text: ARG is available at run time; ENV is only at build time
ARG is a build-time variable that is gone at run time; ENV is baked into the image and available while the container runs
They are identical
Both are safe places to store secrets

prompt: What is the recommended way to make one image behave differently in dev vs production?
explanation: Environment variables (-e or --env-file) let the same image run everywhere, with only the configuration changing — a core twelve-factor idea.

options.text: Build a separate image per environment with the config hard-coded
Pass configuration through environment variables at run time
Edit the running container's files by hand
Use a different base image each time

prompt: Which restart policy restarts a container after crashes and host reboots but respects a manual docker stop?
explanation: unless-stopped behaves like always but does not restart the container if you deliberately stopped it.

options.text: no
on-failure
unless-stopped
always-even-when-stopped

prompt: docker stop first sends the ______ signal to allow a graceful shutdown before forcing SIGKILL. (signal name)
explanation: docker stop sends SIGTERM first, then SIGKILL after a grace period (10 seconds by default) if the process has not exited.

prompt: Which statements are true about configuration and exit codes? Select all that apply.
explanation: 0 means success, ARG/ENV are not safe for secrets, and --env-file loads variables in bulk. The default restart policy is 'no', so stopped containers stay stopped.

options.text: An exit code of 0 means the container exited successfully
Secrets should not be passed via ARG or ENV expecting them to be hidden
--env-file loads many environment variables from a file
By default, a container that stops is automatically restarted

prompt: Match each restart policy to its behavior.
explanation: The four policies range from never restarting to always restarting, with on-failure and unless-stopped covering the common middle-ground cases.

pairs.right: Never restart (the default)
Restart only on a non-zero exit code
Restart whenever it stops, including on reboot
Like always, but not after a manual stop

prompt: What is a Docker image made of?
explanation: An image is a stack of read-only layers. Layers are shared across images and cached during builds, which saves space and time.

options.text: A single compressed file with no internal structure
A stack of read-only layers, each a set of filesystem changes
A running process and its memory
A virtual machine disk image

prompt: What is the difference between a tag and a digest?
explanation: A tag like 1.27 or latest can be re-pointed to a new image. A digest (sha256 hash) always refers to the exact same image bytes.

options.text: A tag is immutable; a digest can change
A tag is a movable label; a digest is an immutable content hash of the exact image
They are two words for the same thing
A digest is only used for private images

prompt: Why is depending on the `latest` tag risky for reproducibility?
explanation: latest is a movable label, not a version. The same reference can resolve to a different image over time, which undermines reproducibility.

options.text: latest images are always broken
latest is not a fixed version; it is whatever was most recently tagged, so it can change silently
latest images cannot be pulled
latest always points to the oldest version

prompt: Docker's curated official images live in the special ______ namespace, which is why you can reference them by a bare name like nginx. (one word)
explanation: Official images live in the library namespace, so nginx, library/nginx, and docker.io/library/nginx:latest all mean the same image.

prompt: Which are good practices when choosing and referencing images? Select all that apply.
explanation: Pin versions or digests and prefer trusted (official/verified) images. Popularity alone is not a substitute for checking the publisher.

options.text: Pin an explicit version tag instead of relying on latest
Pin a digest when you need byte-for-byte reproducibility
Prefer official or verified base images
Always use the newest random image with the most stars, regardless of publisher

prompt: Match each part of docker.io/library/nginx:1.27 to what it is.
explanation: A full reference is registry/namespace/repository:tag. Missing parts default to docker.io, library, and latest.

pairs.right: The registry host
The namespace (official images)
The repository name
The tag (version label)

prompt: What is a container registry?
explanation: A registry stores and distributes images. Docker Hub is the default public registry; GHCR and cloud/self-hosted registries are common alternatives.

options.text: A tool that builds images
A server that stores and distributes images, which you push to and pull from
A type of container network
The writable layer of a container

prompt: To push an image to GitHub Container Registry, how must it be named?
explanation: A registry-qualified name like ghcr.io/owner/repo:tag tells docker push which registry and repository to upload to.

options.text: hello:latest
ghcr.io/<owner>/<repo>:<tag>
github.com/<owner>/<repo>
docker.io/hello

prompt: Does docker tag copy the image?
explanation: docker tag adds an additional reference to an existing image without copying it. One image can carry many tags simultaneously.

options.text: Yes, it makes a full duplicate
No, it only adds another name pointing at the same image
Only for images larger than 1 GB
Only when pushing to Docker Hub

prompt: The strongest way to guarantee you deploy an exact, unchanging image is to reference it by its ______. (one word)
explanation: A digest (repo@sha256:...) is immutable and always resolves to the identical image bytes, even if tags are later moved.

prompt: Which are good tagging or registry practices? Select all that apply.
explanation: Pin versions, add SHA tags for traceability, and use scoped tokens safely. latest is a moving label and should not be the production source of truth.

options.text: Tag releases with a specific semantic version
Add a git-SHA tag in CI for traceability
Authenticate with a scoped token passed via --password-stdin
Deploy :latest to production as the source of truth

prompt: Order the steps to publish a local image to a registry.
explanation: Authenticate, give the image a registry-qualified name, push it, and then it can be pulled by others.

items.text: docker tag the image with a registry-qualified name
A teammate pulls it by that name or digest

prompt: What is the difference between RUN and CMD?
explanation: RUN executes during the build and its result becomes an image layer. CMD sets the default command that runs each time a container starts from the image.

options.text: RUN runs when the container starts; CMD runs at build time
RUN executes at build time and is baked into the image; CMD is the default command run when a container starts
They are identical
CMD can appear many times and all of them run

prompt: Does the EXPOSE instruction publish a port so your machine can reach the container?
explanation: EXPOSE is documentation/metadata only. To actually reach the container's port from your machine you publish it with -p host:container at run time.

options.text: Yes, EXPOSE opens the port to the host
No, EXPOSE only documents the port; you still publish it at run time with -p
Yes, but only for port 80
No, EXPOSE disables the port

prompt: In `docker build -t mysite:1.0 .`, what does the trailing dot mean?
explanation: The dot is the build context: the directory Docker packages and sends to the daemon. COPY can only copy files inside this context.

options.text: It hides the build output
It is the build context — the directory sent to the daemon that COPY reads from
It means 'use the latest tag'
It is optional decoration

prompt: The file that lists paths to exclude from the build context is called ______. (filename)
explanation: A .dockerignore file keeps files like .git, node_modules, and .env out of the build context, making builds faster and images cleaner.

prompt: Why is the exec form CMD ["node", "server.js"] preferred over the shell form CMD node server.js?
explanation: The exec (JSON-array) form runs the process directly, so it receives Unix signals. The shell form wraps the command in /bin/sh -c, which can swallow SIGTERM and slow down graceful stops.

options.text: It is shorter to type
It runs the program directly so it receives signals like SIGTERM, allowing docker stop to shut it down cleanly
The shell form is not valid Dockerfile syntax
The exec form runs faster at build time

prompt: Order these Dockerfile instructions as they should typically appear for a simple app.
explanation: Start from a base image, set the working directory, copy your files in, then declare the default command to run at container start.

prompt: When one Dockerfile layer's cache is invalidated, what happens to the instructions after it?
explanation: A cache miss cascades: once a layer changes, no layer below it can be reused, so all subsequent instructions run again.

options.text: Nothing; only that one layer rebuilds
Every layer after it is rebuilt too
The build fails
The layers below are skipped entirely

prompt: Why copy the dependency manifest and install dependencies before copying the rest of the source?
explanation: Because a cache miss cascades, putting the rarely-changing dependency install above the frequently-changing source keeps the expensive install layer cached.

options.text: It is required syntax
Dependencies change less often, so that layer stays cached across code edits and installs are skipped
It makes the image larger on purpose
It disables the build cache

prompt: Why combine apt-get install and the cleanup of package lists into a single RUN?
explanation: Cleaning up in a later RUN cannot shrink the image, because the earlier layer already contains the files. Doing it in the same RUN keeps them out.

options.text: It is the only valid syntax
Each RUN is a layer, so cleaning up in the same RUN keeps the removed files out of the image
It runs faster at container start
It publishes the ports automatically

prompt: The instruction that sets the fixed executable a container always runs is ______. (one word)
explanation: ENTRYPOINT fixes the program that runs; CMD supplies default arguments that are easy to override at docker run.

prompt: Which are good Dockerfile practices? Select all that apply.
explanation: Pin versions, use a .dockerignore, and order stable-before-volatile. Copying source before installing deps defeats the cache.

options.text: Pin base image tags instead of using latest
Ship a .dockerignore to keep the context small and safe
Place volatile steps (copying source) after stable ones (installing deps)
Copy all source first, then install dependencies

prompt: Given ENTRYPOINT ["python", "-m", "http.server"] and CMD ["8000"], what does `docker run img 9000` do?
explanation: Arguments after the image override CMD but not ENTRYPOINT, so the server runs on 9000 while the fixed program stays python -m http.server.

options.text: Fails, because you cannot pass arguments
Runs python -m http.server 9000, overriding the CMD default while keeping the ENTRYPOINT
Ignores 9000 and serves on 8000
Replaces the whole command with 9000

prompt: What happens to files written to a container's writable layer when you run docker rm?
explanation: The writable layer is scratch space tied to the container. Removing the container deletes it, so durable data must live in a volume or bind mount.

options.text: They are automatically moved to a volume
They are deleted along with the container
They are pushed to the registry
They stay on the host forever

prompt: Which storage type is the recommended default for persisting a database's data?
explanation: Named volumes are managed by Docker and persist independently of any container, making them the default choice for application and database data.

options.text: A named volume
The container's writable layer
A tmpfs mount
The image's read-only layers

prompt: When is a bind mount the best fit?
explanation: A bind mount maps a specific host folder into the container, so editing source on the host is instantly visible inside — ideal for local development. It is not portable across machines.

options.text: For portable data shared across many machines
For local development, so host edits appear instantly inside the container
For keeping secrets in memory only
It is never useful

prompt: A ______ mount stores data only in the host's memory and never writes it to disk. (one word)
explanation: A tmpfs mount keeps data in memory only; it disappears when the container stops, which suits short-lived sensitive data.

prompt: Which statements about volumes and bind mounts are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: Volumes are Docker-managed and portable; bind mounts are host-path specific; -v silently creates a missing path. A volume persists after its container is removed (that is the point).

options.text: Named volumes are managed by Docker and are portable across machines
Bind mounts depend on exact host paths, so they are not portable
With -v, a missing bind-mount host path is silently created as an empty directory
Data in a named volume is deleted whenever its container is removed

prompt: Match each storage type to its best use.
explanation: Volumes persist app data, bind mounts share host folders for dev, tmpfs keeps data in memory, and the writable layer is temporary per-container scratch space.

pairs.right: Persisting a database's data
Live-editing source code in development
In-memory scratch data never written to disk
Disposable scratch space for one container

prompt: How do you mount a named volume as read-only inside a container?

options.text: Add the :ro suffix to the -v flag, e.g. -v mydata:/app/data:ro
Run chmod -R 444 inside the container
Set READONLY=true in the container environment variables
Volumes cannot be made read-only

explanation: Appending :ro (or readonly with --mount) attaches the volume in read-only mode, blocking write operations by the container process.

prompt: Which flag in docker system prune removes unused named volumes?

options.text: docker volume prune (or docker system prune --volumes)
docker system prune --all (prunes volumes automatically)
docker volume rm --force
docker rmi --volumes

explanation: Because volumes often hold critical persistent state, docker system prune skips volumes unless you pass the --volumes flag or run docker volume prune.

prompt: What is the standard technique for backing up a Docker named volume without stopping services?

options.text: Run an ephemeral container with --volumes-from to mount the volume read-only and stream a tar archive to the host
Directly copy files from /var/lib/docker/volumes while the container is actively writing
Commit the container to an image and push it to a registry
Export the container filesystem with docker export

explanation: Spinning up a transient container mounting the volume and running tar produces a clean, isolated backup archive on the host without risking filesystem corruption.

prompt: Which characteristics are true of tmpfs mounts in Docker? Select all that apply.

options.text: Data is stored strictly in volatile host memory (RAM), never written to host disk
Data is automatically wiped when the container stops
Data survives container deletion and host reboot
tmpfs mounts cannot be shared between multiple containers

explanation: tmpfs mounts exist purely in host RAM. When the container stops, the tmpfs mount is removed and all data is lost. They cannot be shared across containers.

prompt: To inspect the exact host mountpoint and filesystem metadata of a volume named db-data, run `docker volume ______ db-data`.
explanation: `docker volume inspect <name>` returns JSON describing the Driver, Labels, Mountpoint on the host, and creation timestamp.

prompt: Match each volume management command to its purpose.

pairs.right: Allocates a new named storage volume
Lists all existing volumes on the host
Shows detailed volume mountpoint metadata
Removes all unattached storage volumes

explanation: create, ls, inspect, and prune manage the full lifecycle of Docker volumes on a host.

prompt: What is the key advantage of a user-defined bridge network over the default bridge?
explanation: On a user-defined bridge, containers resolve each other by name via built-in DNS. The default bridge supports communication only by IP address.

options.text: It is faster
It provides automatic DNS, so containers can reach each other by container name
It publishes all ports automatically
It disables container isolation

prompt: Do two containers on the same network need a published port to communicate with each other?
explanation: Containers on the same network talk directly over the container port. You publish (-p) only what needs to be reachable from outside.

options.text: Yes, always
No; publishing is only for reaching a container from the host or outside world
Only if they use TCP
Only on the host network

prompt: How should one container refer to another for a reliable connection?
explanation: Use the container/service name on a shared user-defined network. Docker resolves the name via DNS, and names are stable while IPs can change.

options.text: By the other container's IP address, hard-coded
By the other container's name on a shared user-defined network
By the host machine's public IP
By the image digest

prompt: The network mode that gives a container no external networking at all is called ______. (one word)
explanation: The none network mode leaves a container with only loopback and no external connectivity, useful for fully isolated tasks.

prompt: Which statements about Docker networking are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: EXPOSE is documentation, containers can join multiple networks, and -p forwards a host port. Name resolution works on user-defined bridges, not the default bridge.

options.text: EXPOSE in a Dockerfile only documents a port; it does not open it
A container can be connected to more than one network
The default bridge resolves container names via DNS
Publishing with -p forwards a host port to a container port

prompt: Order these steps to run an app and database that talk by name.
explanation: Create the shared network, start both containers on it, and the app resolves the database by its container name db.

items.text: The app connects to the database at hostname db

prompt: What is the IP address of the embedded Docker DNS server inside user-defined networks?
explanation: Dockers embedded DNS server listens on loopback IP 127.0.0.11 inside container network namespaces connected to user-defined networks.

prompt: When using --network host, what happens to network isolation?

options.text: The container shares the host network namespace directly, bypassing all network isolation and port mapping overhead
The container is assigned a private virtual bridge IP
The container cannot bind to ports below 1024
The container is completely cut off from network access

explanation: In host networking mode (--net=host), the container shares the host network stack directly, achieving native speeds at the expense of namespace isolation.

prompt: Why does container DNS resolution fail between two containers running on the default bridge network? Select all that apply.

options.text: The default bridge network does not run the embedded DNS server
Containers on the default bridge can only reach each other by IP address unless legacy links are used
The default bridge blocks all ICMP packets
Containers on the default bridge cannot use TCP

explanation: The default bridge only supports communication via IP addresses or legacy --link flags. Automatic DNS name resolution requires a user-defined network.

prompt: To disconnect a running container named web-app from a network named frontend-net, use the command `docker network ______ frontend-net web-app`.
explanation: `docker network disconnect <network> <container>` detaches a container from a network dynamically without stopping the container.

prompt: Order the steps to troubleshoot a container DNS resolution failure.

items.text: Verify both containers are attached to the same user-defined network
Run docker exec alpine nslookup target-service to query 127.0.0.11
Test direct IP connectivity using ping or curl against the resolved IP
Check that the target application inside the destination container is listening on the expected port

explanation: Troubleshoot network issues starting from network membership, DNS lookup, raw IP connectivity, and finally service port binding.

prompt: Match each Docker network driver to its core characteristic.

pairs.right: Default host-isolated private virtual Ethernet network
Shares the host network stack directly with zero isolation
Completely disables all network interfaces except loopback
Assigns each container a unique physical MAC address on the LAN

explanation: Each network driver configures network namespaces, iptables, and virtual interfaces according to different deployment and performance requirements.

prompt: What problem do multi-stage builds solve?
explanation: A multi-stage build does the heavy work in an early stage, then copies only the finished artifact into a lean final stage, leaving compilers and dev dependencies behind.

options.text: They make containers start on multiple hosts
They keep build tools and dev dependencies out of the final image by building in one stage and shipping only the artifact from another
They publish ports automatically
They replace the need for a registry

prompt: In a multi-stage build, which stage(s) end up in the shipped image?
explanation: Only the final stage becomes the image. Earlier stages are used during the build and then discarded.

options.text: All stages combined
Only the last stage
Only the first stage
A random stage chosen at build time

prompt: Why do smaller images improve security, not just speed?
explanation: Less software in the image means fewer components that could contain exploitable vulnerabilities — a smaller attack surface — on top of faster transfers and startup.

options.text: They encrypt the filesystem
Fewer packages mean a smaller attack surface with fewer potential vulnerabilities
They run as root by default
They disable networking

prompt: To copy a built artifact from an earlier stage named build, you write COPY ______=build /app/dist /dest. (the flag)
explanation: COPY --from=build copies from the earlier stage named build rather than from the build context.

prompt: What is a defining characteristic of a distroless base image?
explanation: Distroless images strip out the shell, package manager, and most of the OS, leaving just enough to run your app — very secure, but harder to debug interactively.

options.text: It includes a full desktop environment
It contains only your app and its runtime, with no shell or package manager
It can only run on Windows
It automatically scales your app

prompt: Order the stages of a typical multi-stage build for a compiled or bundled app.
explanation: Start a build stage with the full toolchain, build the artifact, start a minimal runtime stage, then copy just the artifact into it.

items.text: FROM a full toolchain image AS build
Install dependencies and build the artifact
FROM a minimal runtime base image

prompt: What is BuildKit?
explanation: BuildKit is the modern build engine, and it is the default in current Docker. It builds stages in parallel, caches more granularly, and supports mounts and build secrets.

options.text: A registry for storing images
Docker's modern, default build engine with parallel stages, smarter caching, and features like cache mounts
A container orchestration platform
A logging driver

prompt: What does adding `# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1` as the first line do?
explanation: The syntax directive selects the current stable Dockerfile frontend, unlocking features such as cache mounts and build secrets regardless of Docker version.

options.text: It publishes the image
It tells BuildKit to use the current Dockerfile frontend, enabling modern features like RUN --mount
It sets the base image
It runs the container as non-root

prompt: Why build multi-platform images?
explanation: A single-architecture image will not run on a different architecture without emulation. A multi-platform image (a manifest list) provides the right build for each machine.

options.text: To make images larger
Because build and deploy machines can differ in CPU architecture (e.g. arm64 vs amd64), and one multi-platform image runs on each
To avoid using a registry
To disable the cache

prompt: The extended build command that manages builders and produces multi-platform images is docker ______. (one word)
explanation: docker buildx, built on BuildKit, manages builders and can produce multi-platform images with --platform.

prompt: Why does a multi-platform buildx build usually require --push rather than loading locally?
explanation: The local store is single-architecture, so a multi-platform result cannot be loaded into it; you push the manifest list to a registry (or use --load for a single platform).

options.text: Because pushing is faster
Because the local image store holds a single architecture, so the multi-platform manifest list is pushed to a registry instead
Because buildx cannot build locally at all
Because --push disables the cache

prompt: What does a cache mount (RUN --mount=type=cache) do?
explanation: A cache mount keeps a download cache (pip, npm, apk) available across builds for speed, while keeping it out of the final image layers.

options.text: It bakes the package cache into the image as a layer
It persists a package manager's cache across builds without adding it to the image
It publishes the container's ports
It scans the image for vulnerabilities

prompt: What is Docker Compose used for?
explanation: Compose describes a multi-container app in compose.yaml and lets you start, stop, and manage all of it with commands like docker compose up and down.

options.text: Building a single image faster
Defining and running a multi-container application from one YAML file, managed as a unit
Replacing the Docker daemon
Scanning images for vulnerabilities

prompt: How do services in a Compose project reach one another?
explanation: Compose puts all services on a shared project network with DNS, so a service connects to another by its service name (for example, db).

options.text: By hard-coded IP addresses
By service name over the network Compose creates for the project
Only if every port is published to the host
They cannot communicate

prompt: Should a modern Compose file include a top-level `version: "3"` key?
explanation: The top-level version key is obsolete under the current Compose Specification. Compose warns if you include it; leave it out.

options.text: Yes, it is required
No, it is obsolete under the Compose Specification and should be omitted
Only for databases
Only when using build:

prompt: The current Compose command is two words: docker ______ up. (one word)
explanation: Compose v2 is a plugin invoked as docker compose (with a space). The old standalone docker-compose (v1) is retired.

prompt: Does depends_on wait until the dependency is ready to accept connections?
explanation: depends_on controls the order services start, not whether a dependency is ready. Waiting for readiness requires a healthcheck plus condition: service_healthy.

options.text: Yes, it always waits for full readiness
No, it only controls start order; readiness needs a healthcheck and a condition
Yes, but only for databases
No, it has no effect at all

prompt: Which statements about a Compose file and its commands are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: Services can build or use an image, down tears the app down, and --build forces a rebuild. You only publish the ports you need reachable from the host.

options.text: A service can build from a Dockerfile or use a prebuilt image
docker compose down removes the app's containers and network
docker compose up --build rebuilds services that have a build section
You must publish every service's port for the app to work

prompt: What does a healthcheck do in Compose?
explanation: A healthcheck runs a test command on an interval and marks the container healthy, unhealthy, or starting based on the result.

options.text: It publishes the container's ports
It runs a probe command periodically to report the container as healthy or unhealthy
It restarts the host
It builds the image

prompt: How do you make a web service wait until its database is truly ready?
explanation: depends_on alone only orders startup. Combined with a healthcheck and condition: service_healthy, the dependent service waits until the dependency reports healthy.

options.text: Use depends_on alone
Give the database a healthcheck and set depends_on with condition: service_healthy on the web service
Publish the database port
Add a sleep to the database image

prompt: What are Compose profiles used for?
explanation: A service with profiles: ["debug"] starts only when you activate that profile (docker compose --profile debug up), which suits optional debuggers, seeders, and migrations.

options.text: Encrypting the Compose file
Including a service only when its profile is activated, for optional tools or one-off jobs
Setting the base image
Publishing ports automatically

prompt: To load environment variables into a service from a separate file, use the ______ key. (one word, with underscore)
explanation: env_file loads variables from a separate file, keeping configuration and secrets out of the committed Compose file.

prompt: What does `docker compose config` print?
explanation: docker compose config resolves overrides and ${VAR} interpolation and prints the final configuration, which is invaluable for debugging multi-file setups.

options.text: The Docker daemon logs
The fully merged and interpolated configuration, so you can verify overrides and variables
A list of images on Docker Hub
The container's health status

prompt: Which statements about advanced Compose features are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: Networks isolate tiers, override files layer config, and ${VAR:-default} supplies a fallback. A probe that only checks the process is running is not a real readiness check.

options.text: Custom networks can isolate tiers so a frontend cannot reach a backend-only service
Override files let you layer environment-specific changes on a shared base
${WEB_PORT:-8080} substitutes WEB_PORT or defaults to 8080
A healthcheck that only checks the process exists is a thorough readiness probe

prompt: By default, what user does a container's process run as, and why is that a concern?
explanation: Unless the image sets a USER, the process runs as root. Running unprivileged limits what an attacker can do if the app is compromised.

options.text: A random user; it is never a concern
root (unless a USER is set); a compromise then gives an attacker root inside the container
nobody; it is fully safe
The host's logged-in user

prompt: Why can't you hide a secret by COPYing it into an image and deleting it in a later instruction?
explanation: Each instruction adds a layer; the secret remains in the earlier layer and can be extracted, even if a later instruction appears to remove the file.

options.text: Because Docker encrypts all layers
Because the secret is stored in the layer created by the COPY, and later layers do not erase earlier ones
Because deletes are not allowed in Dockerfiles
It actually does hide the secret safely

prompt: How do you provide a secret during a build without baking it into the image?
explanation: A BuildKit build secret is mounted only for that RUN and never written to a layer, unlike ARG or ENV which persist in the image.

options.text: Pass it with ARG
Use a BuildKit build secret: RUN --mount=type=secret with docker build --secret
Set it as an ENV
COPY it in and delete it

prompt: Docker's built-in tool for scanning images for known vulnerabilities is Docker ______. (one word)
explanation: docker scout cves <image> lists known CVEs in an image's packages; scanning belongs in CI so vulnerable images are caught early.

prompt: Which practices apply least privilege to a container? Select all that apply.
explanation: Read-only filesystems, dropped capabilities, and no-new-privileges all reduce privilege. --privileged does the opposite, removing most isolation.

options.text: Run with --read-only and mount a small tmpfs for paths that need writes
Use --cap-drop ALL and add back only the capabilities needed
Add --security-opt no-new-privileges
Run with --privileged to be safe

prompt: Which base-image habit best reduces the number of vulnerabilities you ship?
explanation: Minimal images have a smaller attack surface, trusted/pinned images are predictable, and regular rebuilds pull in upstream security patches.

options.text: Use the largest possible base image
Prefer minimal, trusted, pinned base images and rebuild regularly to pick up patches
Always use :latest and never rebuild
Avoid official images

prompt: What is the recommended practice for handling Linux capabilities on production containers?

options.text: Drop all capabilities with --cap-drop=ALL, then selectively add back only required ones with --cap-add
Run containers with --privileged so capabilities are automatically handled
Linux capabilities do not apply to Docker containers
Always add CAP_SYS_ADMIN for optimal container performance

explanation: Applying least privilege by dropping all kernel capabilities (--cap-drop=ALL) and adding back only specific necessary capabilities minimizes attack surface.

prompt: Why is mounting the Docker host socket (/var/run/docker.sock) into an untrusted container dangerous?

options.text: It gives the container full root access over the host Docker daemon, allowing root host compromise
It causes high memory consumption on the host kernel
It prevents the container from writing logs
It slows down container startup times

explanation: Access to the Docker socket allows creating privileged containers with host root mounted (-v /:/host), granting full root-level control over the underlying host machine.

prompt: How does mounting the container root filesystem as read-only (--read-only) improve security?

options.text: It prevents attackers from modifying application binaries, downloading malware, or altering system files
It compresses the container image on disk
It speeds up network data transfers
It prevents Docker from reading environment variables

explanation: An immutable root filesystem (--read-only) ensures that even if an attacker achieves remote code execution, they cannot persist malicious scripts or overwrite system binaries.

prompt: Which practices prevent accidental secrets exposure in Docker? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use BuildKit secret mounts (RUN --mount=type=secret) during image builds
Add sensitive files like .env and private keys to .dockerignore
Pass production database passwords via Dockerfile ARG instructions
Inject runtime credentials via environment variables or secret managers instead of baking them into images

explanation: ARG values are recorded in image history and visible via docker history. Use BuildKit secret mounts for build-time secrets and environment injection for runtime.

prompt: To scan a local container image named my-app:latest for security vulnerabilities and CVEs, use the open-source CLI tool named ______.
explanation: Trivy is a popular open-source vulnerability scanner for container images, filesystems, and Git repositories.

prompt: Match each container security flag to its defense mechanism.

pairs.right: Strips all default Linux kernel capabilities from the container
Mounts container root filesystem as immutable
Prevents setuid and setgid binaries from elevating privileges
Executes container process under an unprivileged user UID and GID

explanation: Combining non-root users, no-new-privileges, dropped capabilities, and read-only filesystems forms defense-in-depth container hardening.

prompt: Where should a containerized app send its logs by convention?
explanation: Apps should log to stdout/stderr so Docker (or an orchestrator) captures and routes the logs. docker logs then shows them, and the platform can collect them centrally.

options.text: To a log file inside the container
To standard output and standard error, which Docker captures
Directly to a remote database
Nowhere; containers cannot log

prompt: A container exited with code 137 and OOMKilled is true. What does that mean?
explanation: Exit code 137 with OOMKilled true indicates the container was killed for running out of memory, so the fix is more memory or a leaner workload.

options.text: The application had a syntax error
The container exceeded its memory limit and was killed
The image failed to download
The port was already in use

prompt: What is the difference between a container being 'running' and being 'healthy'?
explanation: A container can be running while the app inside is wedged. A HEALTHCHECK tests real functionality and reports healthy or unhealthy.

options.text: There is no difference
Running means the process started; healthy means a HEALTHCHECK probe confirms the app actually works
Healthy means it uses less memory
Running means it passed its healthcheck

prompt: The command that shows a container's full configuration and state as JSON is docker ______. (one word)
explanation: docker inspect dumps the full JSON, including state fields like ExitCode and OOMKilled; use --format to extract specific values.

prompt: How can you debug a container that crashes too quickly to exec into?
explanation: Overriding the entrypoint with a shell lets you start the container, run the real command manually, and see the error with full context.

options.text: You cannot; the image is unusable
Run it with an overridden entrypoint, e.g. docker run -it --entrypoint sh <image>, then investigate
Delete the image and rebuild without changes
Publish more ports

prompt: Which are good logging and debugging practices? Select all that apply.
explanation: Rotate json-file logs, start debugging from logs and exit codes, and use meaningful healthchecks. Logging only to internal files hides output from docker logs and the platform.

options.text: Configure rotation (max-size, max-file) for the json-file log driver
Make docker logs and the exit code your first steps when a container fails
Add a HEALTHCHECK that tests a real endpoint
Write logs only to files inside the container

prompt: What are the three pillars of observability?
explanation: The three pillars are logs (events), metrics (numbers over time), and traces (a single request's path across services).

options.text: Images, containers, and volumes
Logs, metrics, and traces
Build, test, and deploy
CPU, memory, and disk

prompt: Why prefer structured logging over free-form text?
explanation: Structured logs (e.g. JSON with fields) let you query things like 'all status:500 on /orders in the last hour' and aggregate across services — hard with plain text.

options.text: It uses less disk always
Machine-readable records with consistent fields can be filtered, searched, and aggregated across many containers
It disables logging
It is required by Docker

prompt: How does Prometheus collect metrics?
explanation: Prometheus scrapes (pulls) a /metrics endpoint from each service on a schedule and stores the values as time series, often visualized in Grafana.

options.text: Services push metrics to it over email
It uses a pull model, scraping each service's /metrics endpoint on a schedule
It reads them from the Dockerfile
It does not collect metrics

prompt: A ______ probe decides whether to send a container traffic, while a liveness probe decides whether to restart it. (one word)
explanation: A readiness probe controls whether traffic is sent; a liveness probe controls whether the container is restarted. They answer different questions.

prompt: Which question is each observability pillar best at answering?
explanation: Metrics detect and trend a problem, traces localize where the time or failure is across services, and logs explain why it happened.

options.text: Logs say where, metrics say why, traces say if
Metrics say something is wrong, traces say where, logs say why
They all answer the same question
Metrics say why, logs say where, traces say nothing

prompt: Which are good observability practices? Select all that apply.
explanation: Alert on user-facing symptoms, use structured logs, and separate liveness from readiness. Metrics are what you dashboard and alert on, so logs alone are not enough.

options.text: Alert on symptoms users feel, like error rate and latency (SLOs)
Emit structured logs to stdout and ship them to a central store
Implement distinct liveness and readiness probes
Rely on logs alone and skip metrics entirely

prompt: What best describes DevOps?
explanation: DevOps is primarily a culture of shared ownership and fast feedback, supported by automation — not just a tool or product.

options.text: A single tool you install
A culture and set of practices uniting development and operations through shared ownership, automation, and fast feedback
A programming language
A type of container

prompt: What is the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?
explanation: Both make passing changes releasable. Delivery keeps a manual gate before production; deployment removes that gate and ships automatically.

options.text: They are the same thing
Continuous delivery keeps a human approval before the production deploy; continuous deployment deploys every passing change automatically
Continuous delivery skips testing
Continuous deployment never reaches production

prompt: Why is a container image an ideal artifact for a CI/CD pipeline?
explanation: An image is an immutable, versioned artifact bundling app and dependencies, so the thing you tested is exactly the thing you deploy.

options.text: Because it must be rebuilt for each environment
Because it is immutable and versioned, so you build once and promote the exact same image from staging to production
Because it stores configuration inside the image
Because it cannot be pushed to a registry

prompt: The practice of merging small changes frequently with an automated build and test on each is called continuous ______. (one word)
explanation: Continuous integration merges changes often and runs automated build and tests to catch integration problems early.

prompt: Which twelve-factor habits help containers thrive in CI/CD? Select all that apply.
explanation: Config in the environment, stateless processes, and logs as streams all fit the container model. Baking secrets into the image is the opposite of good practice.

options.text: Keep configuration in the environment, not baked into the image
Keep processes stateless, storing state in backing services
Write logs to stdout/stderr as event streams
Hard-code production secrets into the image

prompt: Order the typical stages of a CI/CD pipeline.
explanation: After a commit triggers the pipeline, it builds, tests, packages/publishes the image, and then deploys and operates it.

items.text: Package it as a container image and push to a registry

prompt: Where do GitHub Actions workflow files live?
explanation: Workflows are YAML files placed in .github/workflows/. Each defines events, jobs, and steps.

options.text: In the repository root as action.yml
In the .github/workflows/ directory as YAML files
In a Docker image
In the registry

prompt: What permission must a job have to push an image to GHCR, and what token does it use?
explanation: Pushing to GHCR requires permissions: packages: write. The job authenticates with the automatic GITHUB_TOKEN via docker/login-action.

options.text: contents: write, using a personal SSH key
packages: write, using the automatic GITHUB_TOKEN
No permission is needed
admin: write, using a hard-coded password

prompt: How do you ensure the image is built and pushed only after tests pass?
explanation: needs: test makes the build-and-push job depend on the test job, so no image is published when tests fail.

options.text: Put both in the same step
Give the build job needs: test so it runs only if the test job succeeds
Run the build job first
Disable tests

prompt: In a workflow, a repository secret named API_KEY is referenced as ${{ ______.API_KEY }}. (one word)
explanation: Secrets are read via ${{ secrets.NAME }}; they must never be hard-coded in the workflow file.

prompt: What does docker/metadata-action do in a build workflow?
explanation: metadata-action computes useful tags and labels (commit SHA, branch, semantic version) that you feed into build-push-action.

options.text: It runs the container
It generates image tags and labels automatically, such as a SHA tag and a semantic-version tag
It scans for vulnerabilities
It deploys to production

prompt: Which are good practices for a container CI/CD workflow? Select all that apply.
explanation: Test broadly, gate the build on tests, and cache for speed. Credentials belong in secrets, never hard-coded in the workflow.

options.text: Run tests on every push and pull request
Gate the image build behind passing tests with needs:
Cache builds with cache-from/cache-to type=gha
Hard-code your registry password in the YAML

prompt: Why do immutable container images make rollbacks reliable?
explanation: Each version is an immutable image, so a deploy is 'run the new image' and a rollback is 'run the previous one' — both are simple and repeatable.

options.text: Because you patch the running server in place
Because rolling back just means running the previous image (by digest); nothing is modified in place
Because images cannot fail
Because rollbacks require rebuilding from source

prompt: What is the main drawback of the recreate strategy?
explanation: Recreate stops the old version before starting the new one, so there is a gap with downtime. It is simple and fine when brief downtime is acceptable.

options.text: It needs double the resources
There is downtime between stopping the old version and starting the new one
It cannot roll back
It runs three versions at once

prompt: What must you be careful about during a rolling update?
explanation: A rolling update replaces instances gradually, so old and new versions coexist for a while and must be compatible, particularly around database schema changes.

options.text: Only one version ever runs
Both versions run at the same time, so they must be compatible (especially with a shared database)
It always causes downtime
It cannot be rolled back

prompt: Releasing a new version to a small percentage of users first, then expanding based on metrics, is called a ______ deployment. (one word)
explanation: A canary deployment limits the blast radius by exposing the new version to a small fraction of traffic before ramping up.

prompt: How does blue-green deployment enable near-instant rollback?
explanation: Blue-green keeps both environments; traffic is switched to green, but blue stays ready so you can switch back instantly if needed.

options.text: By deleting the old version immediately
By keeping the old (blue) environment running and switching traffic back to it if the new (green) one misbehaves
By rebuilding the image faster
By skipping health checks

prompt: Match each deployment strategy to its defining trait.
explanation: Each strategy trades off downtime, resource usage, and rollback speed differently; choose based on the change's risk.

pairs.right: Stop old, then start new (brief downtime)
Replace instances gradually, no downtime
Two environments; switch traffic all at once
Small percentage first, expand on good metrics

prompt: What is container orchestration?
explanation: An orchestrator runs and manages containers across many machines, handling placement, scaling, self-healing, service discovery, and load balancing.

options.text: A tool for building images faster
Software that manages containers across a cluster of machines — scheduling, scaling, self-healing, and more
A registry for storing images
A way to write Dockerfiles

prompt: What is the desired-state model?
explanation: Orchestrators are declarative: you state the desired state, and a control loop keeps correcting drift (crashes, node failures) to maintain it.

options.text: You issue step-by-step imperative commands to start each container
You declare the goal (e.g. 5 healthy replicas) and the orchestrator continuously reconciles reality to match it
The orchestrator picks a random number of replicas
You must manually restart failed containers

prompt: Why is plain Docker Compose not a substitute for an orchestrator?
explanation: Compose is great for one host, but it does not provide multi-host scheduling, cross-node self-healing, or autoscaling — that is what orchestrators add.

options.text: Compose cannot run more than one container
Compose runs a multi-container app on a single host; it does not spread work across machines or reschedule after a node fails
Compose does not support volumes
Compose cannot use images

prompt: An orchestrator automatically restarting crashed containers and rescheduling those from failed nodes is called ______. (hyphenated word)
explanation: Self-healing restores the desired state by replacing failed containers and rescheduling workloads from dead nodes onto healthy ones.

prompt: How do Docker Swarm and Kubernetes compare at a high level?
explanation: Swarm is easy and built into Docker for small clusters; Kubernetes is far more powerful and the industry standard, but more complex.

options.text: Swarm is the industry standard; Kubernetes is built into Docker
Swarm is simpler and built into Docker; Kubernetes is more powerful, the industry standard, with a steeper learning curve
They are identical
Neither can self-heal

prompt: Which capabilities do orchestrators typically provide? Select all that apply.
explanation: Orchestrators schedule, scale, self-heal, and provide service discovery and load balancing. They run your app; they do not write it.

options.text: Scheduling containers onto suitable nodes
Scaling the number of replicas up or down
Service discovery and load balancing across replicas
Writing your application's business logic for you

prompt: What is a Pod in Kubernetes?
explanation: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit; it wraps one or more containers that share an IP and storage, and is usually a single container in practice.

options.text: A physical server in the cluster
The smallest deployable unit — one or more containers sharing a network identity and storage
A load balancer
The control plane

prompt: What does a Deployment provide?
explanation: A Deployment declares the desired Pods (image and replica count) and manages a ReplicaSet to scale, self-heal, and roll out updates.

options.text: A stable network address for Pods
Management of a set of identical Pods, including scaling, self-healing, and rolling updates
Storage for cluster state
The container runtime

prompt: Why do you need a Service when you already have Pods?
explanation: Because Pods come and go with changing IPs, a Service provides a fixed name/IP and spreads traffic across the matching Pods.

options.text: Pods cannot run containers without one
Pods are ephemeral and change IPs; a Service gives a stable address and load-balances across the current Pods
A Service builds the image
A Service stores secrets

prompt: The command-line tool used to talk to a Kubernetes cluster is ______. (one word)
explanation: kubectl is the CLI for the API server; the declarative workflow is kubectl apply -f manifest.yaml.

prompt: How does the Docker image you built relate to Kubernetes?
explanation: Kubernetes schedules and runs the same OCI image you built and pushed; the kubelet pulls it and runs it in a container inside a Pod.

options.text: Kubernetes rebuilds your app from source
Kubernetes runs the exact OCI image you pushed; a Deployment's image field points at your registry
Kubernetes cannot use Docker images
You must convert the image to a special Kubernetes format

prompt: Match each Kubernetes concept to its role.
explanation: The control plane decides, nodes run workloads, Deployments maintain Pods, and Services expose them with a stable endpoint.

pairs.right: Manages the cluster and desired state
A worker machine that runs Pods
Keeps a set of identical Pods running
Stable address and load balancing for Pods

prompt: What is Infrastructure as Code (IaC)?
explanation: IaC defines and manages infrastructure through version-controlled files, making it repeatable, reviewable, and recoverable.

options.text: Writing application business logic
Managing infrastructure through machine-readable, version-controlled files instead of manual clicks or ad-hoc commands
A type of container image
A registry for storing servers

prompt: What is the difference between declarative and imperative infrastructure?
explanation: Declarative definitions state the goal and let the tool reconcile to it (safe to re-apply); imperative definitions script the exact steps and order.

options.text: Declarative lists the steps; imperative lists the end state
Declarative describes the desired end state and is idempotent; imperative specifies the ordered steps you run yourself
They are the same
Imperative is always safer

prompt: How should secrets be handled in IaC?
explanation: Configuration lives in code, but secrets must not sit in plain text in the repo; store them in a secrets manager (or platform secret mechanism) and reference them.

options.text: Commit them in plain text so they are versioned
Keep them out of the files and store them in a secrets manager, referencing them instead
Email them to the team
Bake them into the base image

prompt: When a live system diverges from its defined desired state, that gap is called configuration ______. (one word)
explanation: Configuration drift happens when manual, out-of-band changes make the running system differ from its definitions; declarative IaC and GitOps detect and correct it.

prompt: What is GitOps?
explanation: In GitOps the desired state lives in Git; an automated agent reconciles the system to match, so changes are made via pull requests and drift is auto-corrected.

options.text: A way to write Dockerfiles
An approach where Git is the source of truth and an agent continuously reconciles the live system to match it
A Git hosting service
A container runtime

prompt: Which are benefits of Infrastructure as Code? Select all that apply.
explanation: IaC makes infrastructure repeatable, reviewable, and auditable. Definitions still need testing — a bad definition can break infrastructure like bad code.

options.text: Repeatable environments from the same files
Changes reviewed through pull requests
Versioned, auditable history with easy rollback
It removes the need to ever test changes

prompt: What is the correct order of the end-to-end workflow?
explanation: The workflow flows from packaging the app to running it locally, publishing it via CI/CD, deploying it, and operating it in production.

options.text: Deploy, operate, containerize, test, build
Containerize, run locally with Compose, CI/CD (build/test/push), deploy, operate
Operate, deploy, run locally, containerize
CI/CD, containerize, operate, run locally

prompt: What does 'promote the image' mean?
explanation: Promotion means moving one immutable, tested artifact through staging to production without rebuilding, so what runs is exactly what passed CI.

options.text: Advertise the image on Docker Hub
Deploy the exact same tested image (by tag or digest) through each environment unchanged
Rebuild the image for each environment
Increase the image's tag number automatically

prompt: In the capstone Compose file, why does the api service use depends_on with condition: service_healthy?
explanation: The readiness gate makes the api wait for the database's healthcheck to pass, so it does not race ahead and fail to connect.

options.text: To publish the database port
So the api starts only after the database reports healthy, avoiding connection errors
To build the database image
To scan for vulnerabilities

prompt: To recover from a bad deployment, you redeploy the ______ image or digest, since old versions are kept available. (one word)
explanation: Because you deploy immutable images and keep old ones, rollback is redeploying the previous image/digest — fast and reliable.

prompt: Which practices does the capstone Dockerfile combine? Select all that apply.
explanation: It uses multi-stage builds, a non-root user, a healthcheck, and manifest-before-source ordering. Secrets are never baked into the image.

options.text: A multi-stage build with a slim runtime base
Running as a non-root USER
A HEALTHCHECK and cache-friendly instruction ordering
Baking production secrets into an ENV

prompt: Order what happens to one commit as it flows through the pipeline and deploy.
explanation: Tests gate the build; the built image is pushed; then the exact same image is promoted to deployment and operated.

items.text: The image is built and tagged (version + SHA)
The image is pushed to the registry
That same image is deployed and monitored
